> **Key takeaways**
> - Parents want to see four things: the room, the activity, the instructor and the finished work.
> - A phone, daylight and a steady hand are enough. Skip stock photos.
> - No child appears without a parent's written permission. Hands, backs and empty rooms work well.
> - Keep video short and real: one calm pass through a session.

## Why your photos matter

A parent looking at a class listing is trying to picture their child there. Your title and description tell them what happens. Your photos show them. A clear photo answers questions before a parent asks: Is there room to move? Who runs it? What will my child make?

You don't need a photographer. A recent phone, good light and a plan will get you photos for a kids' class listing that look honest and inviting, while keeping children's privacy safe. For the words that go around the pictures, see our guide to [writing a kids' class listing parents actually book](/blog/how-to-write-a-kids-class-listing-parents-book).

## What parents want to see

Plan four photos before you take fifty.

1. **The room.** A wide shot of your real space, set up and ready for class. This is the photo that tells a parent where their child will be.
2. **The activity.** What kids actually do: paint on a brush, a ball at someone's feet, hands on a keyboard. Show the action, not a posed smile.
3. **The instructor.** The person who teaches, in the middle of teaching. Parents are trusting a person, not a logo. Ask your staff before you use their picture.
4. **The finished work.** The clay pot, the little robot, the painted canvas. This is the "what will my child come home with?" photo.

If you only have time for one, make it the room.

## Light: the easiest win

- **Shoot in daylight.** Open the blinds. Indoors, mid-morning or early afternoon usually gives the most even light.
- **Keep the window beside you or behind you,** not behind your subject. A bright window behind a table turns everything on it into a dark shape.
- **Skip the flash.** It flattens colors and makes a warm room look cold.
- **Outdoors, look for open shade.** The shadow of a tree or a building gives soft, even light with no squinting and no hard shadows.

If a photo looks dark on your phone, it will look darker on a parent's screen. Retake it.

## Angles that make a small space look right

- **Get low.** Shoot from a child's eye level. Small spaces look friendlier from there.
- **Use the corner.** For the wide room shot, stand in a corner and shoot across the room. You fit in more floor and more walls.
- **Hold the phone level.** Tilted walls make a room feel off. Turn on your camera's grid lines to keep lines straight.
- **Get close for detail.** Hands at work, a tray of supplies, a half-finished project. Close shots feel warm and need no faces at all.

Tidy up first: bags, cords and paperwork out of frame; mats, easels and instruments in.

## A simple shot list

For your next session:

- A wide shot of the room, set up, taken from a corner
- Your entrance, so families know which door to look for
- Supplies or equipment laid out before class
- Two or three action shots: hands, backs, or the group from a distance
- The instructor teaching, with their OK
- Finished work on a table or a wall, in good light

Take several of each and keep the sharpest. The same set works well on your [Google Business Profile](/blog/google-business-profile-for-kids-activity-businesses), so you only have to shoot once.

## Short video: one calm pass

A short clip shows what photos can't: the pace and feel of a class.

- **Keep it short.** Under a minute is plenty. Walk slowly through the room, show a few seconds of the activity, end on the finished work.
- **Hold steady.** Use both hands, move slowly, or rest the phone on a shelf.
- **Same privacy rules as photos.** Video catches faces and names more easily than a photo, so watch every second before you share it.

## Keep it real

Stock photos look polished, and parents can tell. A bright photo of your real room beats a perfect photo of somewhere else, and a listing that matches what a family finds on day one builds trust. Use photos you took yourself. Fix the light and the crop, then stop: heavy filters make a real room look fake. Update your photos when the room, the equipment or the instructor changes.

## Privacy and consent for children

Get this right every time. A child's photo on a public page can be seen, saved and shared by anyone.

**Get written permission first.** Before any child appears in a photo or video you share, get written permission from that child's parent or guardian.

**Make photo consent its own opt-in.** Ask about photos and video separately from your sign-up form or waiver, with its own clear yes or no, so a parent can say yes to the class and no to the camera. Keep a list of who said yes and check it before every post.

**Prefer no faces.** Even with permission, you often don't need them. Hands at work, kids seen from behind, a wide shot where no one can be recognized, or the room with no children at all tell the story just as well.

**Never names, never school logos.** No children's names in captions, file names or on-screen text. Crop out school logos on shirts and backpacks, name tags, and anything that tells a stranger where a child goes every day. Check the background, too: a sign-in sheet or a child in the corner can slip in.

**Respect a "no".** If a parent says no, that child stays out of every photo and clip, with no pressure and no questions. If a parent who said yes changes their mind later, take the photo down.

This is general good practice, not legal advice. If you are unsure what applies to you, ask a lawyer.

## How ORYN Quest fits

If you run kids' activities in Southern California, you can apply to ORYN Quest at orynquest.com/vendor-apply, and once approved you can list your classes. It's free to join. Your application's first class asks for a photo, so shoot your list first.

To go live, a listing needs a title, category, dollar price per seat, length, location, at least one photo and a waiver answer. Drafts can skip the photo, and families never see drafts, so you can save a listing now and add photos after your next session.

You can add up to five photos in the form, plus one short video (up to 100 MB) as an optional detail. An optional AI photo coach gives tips but never blocks publishing, so you decide which photos go up. You keep ownership of your photos and brand.

## FAQ

### How many photos should a kids' class listing have?
Enough to show the room, the activity, the instructor and the finished work, so four is a good start. On ORYN Quest a listing needs at least one photo to go live, and you can add up to five.

### Can I use photos of children from my class?
Only with written permission from each child's parent or guardian, asked for as a separate photo opt-in. Even then, hands, backs and wide shots where no one can be recognized are often the better choice.

### Do I need a professional photographer?
No. A recent phone, daylight and a child's-eye angle are enough for most small studios. What matters most is that the photos are real and bright.

### How long should a class video be?
Under a minute is plenty. On ORYN Quest, a listing can include one short video of up to 100 MB.
